title: A Geometric Lens on Physics-Aligned Data Compression
claim: At a fixed bitrate, adding a physics loss shifts compression error between the data space and the derived observable space.
layout: 6 panels in a row: field plus two error maps, for each of two spaces
description: The figure shows a running example on 2D fluid velocity fields, in a single horizontal strip. On the left is a velocity-magnitude map in viridis colors with a colorbar from 0 to about 2. Next to it are two stacked error maps for the velocity norm, one for beta=0.00 (MSE only) and one for beta=0.50 (physics loss). They use a dark-to-bright inferno-style colormap with a shared colorbar from 0 to about 0.35. The right half repeats the layout for vorticity. It has a red-blue diverging map of Q(v)=∂y vx−∂x vy, with a colorbar from about -50 to 50. Beside it are two stacked vorticity error maps for beta=0.00 and beta=0.50, with a colorbar from 0 to about 15. The eye goes first to the swirling vorticity and velocity fields, then to the dark speckled error maps. The reader compares the error intensity between the beta rows.
caption: As a running example, we use 2D velocity fields from PDEBench (Takamoto et al., 2022) with channels (vx, vy). The physical observable is vorticity, Q(v) = ∂yvx −∂xvy. The figure compares pointwise compression errors for the reconstructed velocity field and for the derived vorticity. Two models are trained at the same bitrate, 0.85 bps: β = 0 corresponds to MSE-only training, while β = 0.5 includes the physics loss, where β is the physics weight defined in Section 6. At the same bitrate, the β = 0.5 model changes the relative allocation of error between velocity-space and vorticity-space distortions.
abstract: In AI for Science, physics-informed losses are increasingly used to train learned compressors for scientific data, but their rate-distortion implications remain poorly understood. At fixed bitrate, these objectives often improve preservation of a target physical observable while degrading standard reconstruction fidelity. We develop a local geometric theory showing that this tradeoff is governed by the interaction of latent-space sensitivities induced by the entropy model, the physical observable, and the distortion metric. At each operating point, these induce preferred directions along which compression noise should be suppressed, yielding an anisotropic error-allocation mechanism. When these directions are misaligned, improving the observable at fixed rate necessarily worsens standard distortion, establishing a fundamental limit on simultaneous preservation. We formalise this through a local tangent-space rate-distortion law and introduce a practical alignment diagnostic based on dominant eigenspace overlap. Experiments across scientific domains test the theory and validate that the alignment diagnostic correlates with observed data- and physics-space trade-offs.
